#4837. Etsy Says Gah! The Handmade Marketplace and Playful Fashion Label Team Up on a Home Collection

Since its founding in 2015, Lisa Says Gah has become known for its bowtie-pasta cardigans, checkerboard coats, and swans. Today, the California-based label is releasing its first home collection, which has a similarly playful ethos: “The Lisa Says Gah world really naturally extends into the home,” says founder Lisa Bühler. “Home and clothing ultimately tell the story of who you are.”

A pin board and two eclectic frames from Frame Mavens comprise a third of the collection.

Founder Lisa Bühler co-judged the Etsy Design Awards and selected three winners to co-design Etsy Says Gah!, her brand’s first foray into pieces for the home.

The collection is a collaboration with Etsy, a platform Bühler often uses for her own inspiration (things that make her shout: Gah!). “When you go to Etsy, you’re always going to find something that delights you,” she says.

Lisa Says Gah has stocked independent designers alongside its own line for more than a decade. This year, Bühler co-judged the Etsy Design Awards, and selected three winners to co-design Etsy Says Gah!, a nine-piece collection exclusively available via Etsy. Bühler says she prioritized “unexpected, collected things that you just don’t automatically go to when you think of homeware.”

UK-based Cait Mellor executed Bühler’s mood board through crochet in a floral table runner, a horseshoe decal, and swan coasters.

The home collection’s foundational inspiration comes from Lisa Says Gah’s two fall lines, Pastoral Daze and Swan Dance, which pair horses and swans with paisleys and cabin-inspired knits. Bühler worked with the Etsy designers by sharing mood boards, giving notes when she wanted more of a motif or a different color combination, and trusting each maker with her own medium. “They’re the expert[s],” she says. “The process felt like really trusting and putting it in their hands.”’

Each maker applied the same mood board differently. Jacqueline Sanchez, a Houston-based ceramicist who won this year’s Grand Prize for a vase covered in more than 1,500 hand-applied scales, sculpted the swan in relief on a pale pink vase wound with green vines. She also set a horse’s head in a blue baroque cameo on a cream mug and dotted a wavy platter with tiny fruit as a nod to the brand’s food prints. “[I liked] having the freedom to incorporate elements that feel really true to my work,” says Sanchez. The vase is a piece Bühler keeps coming back to: “You would just be happy to have it on the table without flowers,” she says.

The vase is the piece Bühler keeps coming back to: “You would just be happy to have it on the table without flowers,” she says.

“Because it’s our first home collection, we wanted it to feel like something you collect over time in your house versus a uniform grouping,” says Bühler.

Cait Mellor, a UK-based seller, worked the swan and horse elements into the open grid of filet crochet: swans on a set of coasters, a horseshoe under the word Lucky on a small tapestry, and flowers down a cream table runner. Her goal is to “bring this traditional art form into a more contemporary setting.” Bühler is already picturing the coasters at dinner parties, where “everyone is going to talk about the swans.”

Emma Miller and Kristen Kellar, chosen for their fabric-wrapped frames, focused on color and pattern rather than the animals. They made a burgundy frame with black polka dots on a blue background, a frame featuring blue pixelated flowers that look almost cross-stitched, and a pin board that uses pink fabric crossed with orange ribbon.

The home collection’s foundational inspiration comes from Lisa Says Gah’s two fall lines, Pastoral Daze and Swan Dance, which pair horses and swans with paisleys and cabin-inspired knits.

Bühler didn’t want the nine pieces to look like a matched set. “Because it’s our first home collection, we wanted it to feel like something you collect over time in your house versus a uniform grouping,” she says. Each item costs less than $200, and with the holidays coming—with endless-feeling opportunities for hosting and gifting—now is a great time to start collecting.

#4836. Enterprise blockchain is going to come back from the dead

Opinion by Paul Brody, founder and chief executive, Nightfall Networks

Do you remember Pets.com? It raised $110 million from Amazon and others to build a business where people ordered pet toys and dog food online.

The company crashed and burned, and everyone learned an important lesson: you can’t profitably ship a 50-pound bag of dog food to a customer’s door.

As online retail entrepreneur Ed Baum asked in a 2001 postmortem: “Did Pets.com’s business plan assume the invention of transporters to magically move bags of pet food without shipping costs?”

Please, whatever you do, don’t share this with the people at Chewy; they might not realize their business model doesn’t work. Chewy reported $12.6 billion in sales and $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year.

The real lesson of Pets.com wasn’t that shipping dog food was a bad idea. It’s that the idea arrived before the logistics, customer habits and unit economics required to make it work.

As it was with chew toys and dog food, so it may be with enterprise blockchains.

Collectively, the crypto industry probably incinerated just as much money trying that between 2017 and 2023 as Pets.com. Maybe more. But the dozens of companies that went after enterprise blockchain were not delusional; they were just too early.

It’s not hard to understand the appeal of enterprise blockchain solutions, at least superficially. Nearly all enterprise systems today tend to fail at the boundaries between companies. There are two failure modes: mode 1, the OG failure mode, where collaboration information is constantly out of sync.

In this world, enterprise IT systems are islands, communicating asynchronously with each other by digital text messages and emailed spreadsheets. It’s cheap and easy to set up, if you don’t mind always having slightly wrong information.

Failure mode two is the costly, real-time proprietary integration. Powerful industry leaders politely request their key suppliers and partners to join their closed but always-on networks.

Chewy reported $223 million in net income in its latest fiscal year. Source: Chewy.

These are very costly, but they work well and leave everyone with a kind of business version of Stockholm syndrome, where you come to appreciate the thoroughness and efficiency of the digital choke-hold you are in.

Blockchains offered a better path forward: shared information and business logic across an open ecosystem. All the benefits of a proprietary system in terms of real-time visibility and efficiency, without the lock-in.

Sometime around 2017, this started to look like a very obvious good idea. Investment poured in, consortia launched, press releases were drafted and released, and then pretty much everything crashed and burned. TradeLens, We.Trade, Contour, B3i, ASX Chess, Everledger. All came and went in just a few years.

No company wants their competition to see what they’re doing in detail. Mostly, this meant building a private/permissioned chain and then doing lots of non-blockchain-like things to it and in it to try to keep information private. The results were uniformly slow and expensive and failed to gain traction.

It’s hard to understate the bloodbath of companies and startups that tried and failed to make enterprise blockchain work. A quick web and history search turned up 18 different ones, some of them well-known.

What few survivors of this are left have “de-chained” themselves — giving up the blockchain theater and reverting to a classic software-as-a-service (SaaS) model. Many companies that tried and tested these permissioned enterprise systems as users came away from their experience with a clear learning: we tried blockchain, it didn’t work.

That’s unfortunate because everything is different now.

Blockchains have scale. Ethereum in 2020 handled 1 million transactions a day and costs per transaction periodically spiked to $30-50 when demand was high. Today, most transactions get done under a penny and capacity is ramping toward billions of transactions a day. Nobody talks about the “trilemma” anymore. Ethereum is decentralized and it is scaled.

Related: Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade launches on Sepolia testnet

Finally, there’s the money. It’s all moving onchain. Regulators around the globe have blessed stablecoins and the result is a tsunami of liquidity, with transaction volume reaching almost $1.8 trillion in June.

If we combine the operational benefits of blockchains with the financial ones, we get something that enterprises have never really had before: a single ecosystem where you can not only buy, sell, and move assets, but get paid for them as well.

There was just under $1.8 trillion in adjusted stablecoin transaction volume in June. Source: Visa

The return on investment from every single component of this equation is big. Combined, they can yield colossal advantages. McKinsey partners even found that digital supply chain tools could make inventory reductions of 35-75% possible through better planning.

More conservatively, from my experience in the field, just switching away from the existing cascades of spreadsheets and electronic data interchange (EDI) messages can allow firms to run most supply chains with about 20% less inventory at the same service level. That’s worth billions in working capital in most industries.

It gets better from there. Smart contracts reduce the time required to handle many business contract rules from days to minutes and cut the costs of administration in half.

Microsoft began moving its Xbox video game network onto smart contracts for handling royalties and cut the time to access monthly royalty statements from 45 days to four minutes. All that while handling more than 2 million transactions a day.

And once you have inventories, contracts, purchase orders and invoices onchain, you can go after working capital directly as well.

When you can prove your purchase order originates from a top-quality buyer, you can access credit for less. And when you have full visibility into inventory and delivery status, you can factor receivables immediately and efficiently.

The possibilities and the returns are big. The use cases are obvious. It’s time to try again.

#4835. The 91 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 14 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4834. WNBA Star Gabby Williams Found a Team That Asked What She Wanted. Then She Won a Championship

The 30-year-old shares her philosophy on work-life balance and how she keeps her body strong and healthy on a new episode of The Huddle.

WNBA superstar Gabby Williams is proof that hard work and persistence pay off. Drafted into the league in 2018 by the Chicago Sky, the 30-year-old has been slowly building her résumé ever since—both stateside and abroad—notching her first EuroLeague championship in 2022 with Hungary’s Sopron Basket, being named a WNBA All-Star in 2025, and, finally, winning a WNBA Championship in 2026 with the Golden State Valkyries. (She was named Finals MVP too.)

Yes, 2026 has been a big year for the forward, and she has only a couple more months to rest up before taking on her next challenge: debuting in the Unrivaled league, as part of the Miami-based Laces BC.

“It's three-on-three, so you can't hide,” Gabby tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “The positive feedback that I've heard from people who have done it, [is] that the personal development side is great. Players usually go on to have great W seasons after doing Unrivaled.”

How could Gabby possibly top this past year!? We’ll have to wait to find out, but in the meantime, she opens up about finding a home with the Valkyries, keeping herself healthy and injury-free, and building a life outside of basketball.

Over the years, Gabby has earned the nickname “the French Army knife,” due not only to her dual-citizenship (her dad is American; her mom is French) but also to her versatility on the court.

Her role on many teams has been defined by what the team needed, whether it was creating opportunities or defending the paint. But when she went into free agency and signed with the Valkyries earlier this year, it was the first time Gabby recalls someone in the league asking what she wanted to do.

“I was proud to do whatever the team needed,” Gabby says. “But it was nice to trust myself.” That trust—both in herself and from her team—has obviously paid off. Not only does Gabby say she feels more like herself than she ever has, but she has the championship (the Valkyries’ first) to show for it.

Given how little downtime Gabby takes—she often spends part of her off-season playing abroad—she’s crafted a wellness routine that prioritizes stretching, mobility, and maintenance to keep her body in peak physical condition.

And it starts first thing when she wakes up. “I'm a big foam-roller stretcher, especially as I'm getting older,” she says. “I'll spend a good like 20, 15 minutes first thing in the morning just doing my mobility stuff so that when I come to the gym my body's awake and ready.”

At the gym, Gabby and her trainers prioritize accessory work over big Olympic lifts, to limit the wear and tear on her body.

In the off-season, Gabby shifts from a maintenance mindset to an improvement focus with her workouts. If she wants to strengthen a particular body part or movement pattern (like being more explosive) this is when she has the time and energy to do it.

No matter her training regimen, Gabby ends her day much like she starts it—with recovery. She loves an epsom salt bath and can’t get enough of her Normatec compression therapy.

It might be surprising to hear a WNBA champion say “basketball is not life,” but that’s precisely Gabby’s philosophy when it comes to balancing her priorities.

“I think that's why I've been able to have so much success in basketball is because I've learned how to compartmentalize,” she says. She credits that mindset to the coaching team at the University of Connecticut, where she played in college.

“Coach said, ‘When you're on the court, I want you to be focused. I don't want you to be thinking about school. I don't want you to be thinking about your personal life. So while you're doing your other stuff, don't focus on basketball as much. Find the time for your school. When you're going out, go out, have fun.’”

And so Gabby does just that, whether it’s solving a puzzle or picking up a new book. “It is just the perfect way to consume your mind with something else,” she says of reading. She’s even started a Valkyries book club, but it got a bit sidetracked by, of all things, the playoffs. Luckily, there’s always the 2027 season to start anew.

To hear more from Gabby, including her undying love of figure skating and how she’s upped her style game, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

#4833. Diana Ross at Home: 10 Photos of the Pop Diva Off-Duty

As the breakout star of the Supremes and later a solo sensation, Diana Ross proved herself a force to be reckoned with. The Detroit native’s booming career allowed the singer-slash-actor to fashion her own residences in her own singular style: A statement purple sofa, a shag-lined conversation pit, beaded curtains, and a mirrored piano were among the features that might’ve stood out elsewhere, but all appeared seamlessly at home with The Boss. As she declared in her 1979 anthem of independence: “There’s my chair / I put it there / Everything you see / Is with love and care / It’s my house and I live here.”

Through 12 number-one singles with The Supremes, six number-one hits as a solo artist, a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Recording Academy, and a Presidential Medal of Freedom, Ross apparently managed to maintain a sense of normalcy in her domestic life. “My mom is such a mom,” Ross’s daughter, actor Tracee Ellis Ross, said on The Kelly Clarkson Show. “I had a really regular upbringing.” Read on for a roundup of the icon in her offstage moments.

Ross poses on a floral sofa in her Miami suite in this photo, dated March 17, 1970. It was a big year for the songstress: She performed her final concert as lead singer of The Supremes that January, and her debut solo album was released in June.

The singer unwinds on the sofa during an interview.

When these portraits were snapped, Ross was in the middle of a nine-day run of shows at Miami’s Eden Roc hotel—her official debut solo show after a preview run in Framingham, Massachusetts. “Welcome to the ‘Let’s see if Diana Ross can do it by herself club,’” the vocalist said during the performance, journalist Shirley Eder wrote in a March 20, 1970, issue of The Philadelphia Inquirer. Eder also reported that “Diana takes a long time to unwind after a performance… she screens movies in her suite almost nightly.”

A pregnant Ross leans against her reflective piano.

Ross, eight months pregnant with Tracee in this 1972 photo, leans against the mirrored piano in her Beverly Hills home during an interview about her first film role: Billie Holiday in Lady Sings the Blues, directed by Sidney J. Furie. Ross’s depiction of the jazz singer garnered her a Golden Globe and an Oscar nomination, among other accolades. “She’s the greatest improviser I’ve ever known,” Furie told The Hollywood Reporter in 2021. “Some of the main scenes were improvised…. She was the consummate pro and not a diva at all.”

The musician at home with her daughter Rhonda.

Ross lounges in her Beverly Hills home alongside her eldest child, Rhonda, in 1972. The “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” singer’s career was launched by Motown founder Berry Gordy, and the two shared a relationship that was romantic as well as professional. Rhonda was born in 1971 as a result of that liaison, but Ross married music executive Robert Ellis Silberstein two months into the pregnancy, and he raised Rhonda as his own. The couple welcomed two more daughters together: Tracee, who was born not long after this photo was taken, and Chudney, who was born in 1975.

Ross at home taping an appearance for an ABC special.

In the mid-1970s, The Wiz star was once again photographed on the purple sofa in her Beverly Hills living area, which was complete with a white-shag-lined conversation pit and a mirror-bedecked fireplace. According to a 1972 New York Times profile of the artist, her 6,833-square-foot home had 30-foot-tall ceilings and an Andy Warhol tapestry of Marilyn Monroe. The grounds also hosted a swimming pool and a tennis court.

Ross with daughters Tracee (left) and Rhonda.

The Ross family’s Beverly Hills pad boasted five bedrooms and nine bathrooms. According to The Los Angeles Times, the property was built in 1964 for art collector Donald Factor. Because its walls maximized space for paintings, it was reportedly known in the neighborhood as “the house with no windows.” The conversation pit abutted a window adorned with a beaded curtain, as shown in the background of this photo of Ross with Tracee and Rhonda. Both daughters followed in their mother’s footsteps as performers: Tracee is an actor (who recently won her first Daytime Emmy for the program Solo Traveling with Tracee Ellis Ross), while Rhonda was nominated for a Daytime Emmy for her role in the soap opera Another World.

Ross, flanked by her daughters, cradles infant Chudney.

A newborn Chudney also made an appearance during the mid-’70s shoot, as seen in this snapshot. Ross and Silberstein divorced in 1977, and the singer went on to marry Norwegian businessman Arne Naess Jr. in 1986. With Naess, she welcomed two sons, Ross and Evan. The “I’m Coming Out” singer and her second husband split in 2000.

In 1978, a newly single Ross welcomed Barbara Walters to her Beverly Hills home for an interview about her career and life as a single mother in front of a window overlooking the backyard pool. “Her success has brought her every material comfort,” Walters narrated in the television special. “Believe it or not, within 24 hours before we came here she completely refurnished the living room.” The television special offered a glimpse of the conversation pit, now done up with dark maroon carpet and a navy sofa with white cushions.

Ross dressed to impress for her birthday party.

The “Upside Down” singer celebrated her 38th birthday with a party at her Beverly Hills residence in March 1982, as seen in this glamorous snapshot. Later that year, she released Silk Electric, her 13th studio album, and was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

Ross’s daughters were in attendance, as shown in this photo of her bustling birthday party. The 13-time Grammy nominee sold the Beverly Hills property three years later for $1.75 million. These days, the 82-year-old icon lives at Quarry Farm, a property in Greenwich, Connecticut. In 2021, she released her 25th studio album, Thank You.

#4832. Andy Baraghani’s New NYC Restaurant is Full of Design Surprises

“I’ve always been obsessed with design, since I was a kid,” says Andy Baraghani. “I love how restaurant interiors can take you to a different place.”

At Ditto—the all-day café he is opening in New York’s Flatiron—the chef, cookbook author, and YouTube star has given that obsession free rein. With each design decision—from the vintage glass-prism Holophane pendants in the front window to the intense blue (tinted to match Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue) of the rear dining area’s Venetian plaster walls—he asked himself: “Would I actually do this in my home?” If the answer was yes, it passed the test.

The interior of Ditto, with Venetian plaster walls in a shade matching Benjamin Moore Buckland Blue, and Model S22 chairs from Galvanitas.

For Andy Baraghani, design is something of a family affair. His husband, Keith Pollock, is a former AD editor and now a West Elm executive. But opening a restaurant was never part of the plan. In fact, when Michael Silber, a restaurant investor behind New York hot spots like Borgo, Penny, and Bistrot Ha, approached him with the idea of a laid-back restaurant open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, Baraghani admits his first reaction was: “I have no interest.”

It wasn’t for lack of experience. He had started his career in restaurants—from Chez Panisse in Berkeley, where he worked as a teenager, to Estela in New York—before becoming a food editor at Bon Appetit and winning a James Beard Award for his cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be.

But he bonded with Silber over their shared love of greenmarket cooking and decorating deep dives. When it came to Ditto, he says, he wanted the space to convey his personal style. It helped that he and Silber were on the same page. “Andy and I talked about styles ranging from Bauhaus, de Stijl, and classic modernism to 1970s and ’80s aesthetics from places like Italy and France,” Silber says.

They brought in like-minded collaborators: interior designer Eric Wink and architect Alta Indelman. Wink, a close friend of Baraghani who helped with the design of his and Pollock’s home, says the partners told him that New York’s much-missed City Bakery, which was two blocks uptown from Ditto’s 16th Street location, was an inspiration. “They wanted it to feel casual and approachable, with a bit of a New York diner quality,” Wink says.

Holophane pendant lamps hang in the restaurant’s front window.

The space, in a 1905 former factory (its last incarnation was an agnès b. store), is divided into three zones. In the front section, visitors can shop at a market area with hand-picked groceries. A glossy white counter with Bauhaus curves anchors the middle section; this is where customers line up, take a number, and either carry the food out or dine at laminate-topped tables under a trio of oversized custom fabric pendants. The menu, handwritten on a roll of butcher’s paper and updated daily, features dishes like pomegranate spoon salad and what Baraghani calls “the Platonic ideal of granola,” with tahini, maple syrup, and yogurt drizzled with fig-leaf oil.

The third zone, the one painted blue, features an open kitchen and café tables pulled up to a banquette that runs the length of the room. “There’s that good chaos in the middle and the back is a calmer moment,” says Baraghani.

Indelman, a veteran collaborator with New York restaurateurs like Andrew Tarlow and Gabe Stulman, was tasked with giving the space a utilitarian, high-tech ambience. She clad the walls and the open kitchen in patinated stainless steel and preserved industrial elements like structural arches and polished concrete floors.

But it was Baraghani and Silber who took the lead on honing the visual details of the interiors. “We went through 50 possibilities to find the right chair,” Silber says. The one they selected—a 1960s Dutch industrial chair, the Model S22 from Galvanitas—was sourced from Amsterdam Modern in Los Angeles.

Silber also spent hours on eBay bidding on midcentury ceramic bud vases. “They were each under $20 but put them together on a shelf and you have your own little Giorgio Morandi tableau,” he says.

White wall speakers and a French ceramic mask hang above the banquette, tables, and stools upholstered in Maharam’s Stripe It fabric.

The no-nonsense decor also features white wall speakers, created for the space by sound artist Tom Bloxam, and programmed with playlists created by Michael Scanlon of Chandelier Creative, which oversaw Ditto’s branding. But there are quirkier moments too. When it came to choosing fabric for the custom stools, Baraghani insisted on Maharam’s Stripe It, which he felt had a “Baja California” vibe. “We needed that twist,” he says. For his part, Wink specified his favorite stainless-steel toilet for the restrooms—Neo-Metro’s wall-mounted MiniLoo. “I added a custom wood top to soften it a bit,” Wink says.

Meanwhile, a pair of massive midcentury French ceramic faces that hang on a wall opposite the menu of the day are on loan from Baraghani’s own home. “They anchor the space and add a touch of craft,” he says. “I just knew they needed to be here.”

#4831. The Potential Benefits of Using an Anglo First Name

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Many Psychology Today readers are familiar with the dispiriting findings of studies conducted by social scientists: When they apply for jobs or housing, persons with ethnic minority names (like Lakeisha and Abdullah) are generally treated less well than persons with majority group names (like Daniel and Jennifer).

Will foreigners in the United States and Americans with foreign-sounding names be treated better if they adopt an Anglicized name? Would the immensely successful Nvidia executive Jensen Huang have been less successful in business if he had used his birth name, Jen-Hsun?

Two University of Kansas researchers, Xian Zhao and Monica Biernat, have conducted three studies that investigate the potential benefits that may accrue to foreigners who choose to use an Anglo name.

In the first study, 102 Americans—almost all of them White—looked at four photos of Chinese students who were attending college in the United States. Some participants saw photos that were labeled with an Anglo name like Andrew. Others saw photos that showed a Chinese name like Xiang. The participants used a 7-point scale to rate the similarity of each target “to Americans.”

On average, the pictured individuals with Anglo names were rated as more similar to Americans, and the ones with Chinese names were rated as less similar. The difference wasn’t large—about a half-point on the 7-point scale—but it was statistically significant.

In the second study, more than 400 college professors around the U.S. received an e-mail from “a student from China” who asked to meet and talk about the possibility of assisting with the professor’s research. Some professors received an e-mail in which the student introduced himself as Xian Zhao. Others received an e-mail in which the student introduced himself as “Xian Zhao, but you can call me by my English name Alex.” In every other way, the e-mail requests were identical.

The different names affected the likelihood of getting a response. The “Alex” version received responses from 62 percent of the professors, while the “Xian” version received a response from just 53 percent.

In the third study, 184 undergraduates—almost all of them White—listened to a four-minute mini-lecture about affective forecasting. The lecturer introduced himself as a student from China who was pursuing a doctorate in social psychology at the university. In one version of the recording, the lecturer said, “Hi everyone. My name is Jian.” In another version, he said, “Hi everyone. My name is John” (an Anglicized version of Jian). In every other way, the recorded lectures were identical.

The participants were told to listen carefully to the lecture and then candidly evaluate the speaker because the department was “screening and selecting Ph.D. students to be instructors.” The participants also indicated the degree to which they support components of multiculturalism (wanting to learn from other cultural groups, for example) and the degree to which they believe that people who come to the United States should change their behavior to be more like Americans.

The participants evaluated the lecturer more favorably when he used an Anglo name and less favorably when he used his original Chinese name, but only among participants who rejected multiculturalism and believed foreigners should assimilate to local norms.

The opposite pattern was observed among participants who endorsed multiculturalism and did not endorse assimilationism. Those participants actually evaluated the lecturer more favorably when he used his original Chinese name.

The differences observed in these studies were not large, but the bottom line seems clear: Chinese students in the United States—and perhaps other international students—can potentially benefit by choosing to use an Anglo name, especially in more parochial parts of the country.

This strategy, however, may also have a downside. In an earlier post, I reported the results of a 2018 study conducted by the same two Kansas researchers. In that study, Chinese students in the U.S. who adopted an Anglicized name reported slightly lower levels of self-esteem.

It seems that adopting an Anglo name can be a double-edged sword for foreigners. Some employers may evaluate Jian Li slightly lower than John Lee, but Jian may feel somewhat better about himself than John does.

Zhao, X., & Biernat, M. (2017). Welcome to the U.S. but change your name? Adopting Anglo names and discrimination. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 70, 59-68.

#4830. US sellers drive Bitcoin crash, Jensen plots Nvidia comeback: Hodler’s Digest

Anchorage Digital data suggests the Bitcoin selloff is being driven by US investors. A “war room” has been set up by supporters to reinstate Nvidia boss Jensen Huang.

Bitcoin bottomed after the US midterm elections in 2018 and 2022 — and the great Bitcoin crash of November 2026 looks like history repeating. Bitcoin plunged more than $10,000 this week, and is currently trading at $65,116 for a 12.4% loss.

According to Anchorage Digital researcher David Lawant, the call is coming from inside the house. “BTC sell pressure continues to come primarily from the U.S,” he noted, positing a chart highlighting showing continued heavy net taker sell flow primarily on Coinbase compared with overseas exchanges.

The US spot Bitcoin ETFs have seen heavy outflows, losing $2.35 billion over the past two weeks, and influencer Axel Bitblaze noted that Bitcoin fell in the hour before the US open on all but two of the past fifteen days.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao rebuffed the idea that Binance is behind the crash. “No, Binance did not sell crypto. I bought crypto in the past few days,” he said. He attributed the crash to money shifting to the Anthropic IPO, the Bitcoin ETF outflows, security fears about crypto in general in the wake of the Binance hack, and hot inflation data raising expectations of interest rate hikes. Markets are now pricing in a quarter point Fed hike in December.

Bitcoin fell to a four month low near $62,000 on Sunday but has since rebounded above $65,000. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index fell to 10, which is Extreme Fear.

History provides some good news in that Bitcoin more then doubled in price within 12 months of the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections.

The Financial Times reports that Jensen Huang is plotting a comeback to the top job at Nvidia with allies, following a determined push in Silicon Valley to pressure the board to reinstate him.

Nvidia shares plunged after Huang resigned as CEO and from the board on Nov. 12, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress named as interim CEO. The resignation came shortly after news broke he’d had two other affairs, including one with a subordinate.

Multiple people confirmed Huang has been discussing the idea of returning with confidants, even though an independent probe by the board is examining allegations he was romantically involved with a Chinese spy who helped ferry chips to China.

The FT reported one ally saying that supporters have put together a “war room” to reinstate him. “Everybody that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the source said.

A petition to reinstate Huang has garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including 5,600 current Nvidia employees, along with SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney.

The turmoil at Nvidia has weighed heavily on AI stocks and risk assets like cryptocurrency and the story still has a long way to run, with Congressional moves to investigate the issue and three bills being advanced to tighten AI chip export restrictions to China. According to the New York Time, intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Trump about the allegations Alice Huang was a Chinese spy a year ago, but he did not take any action.

Ethereum research group Ethlabs is withdrawing its Quick Slots proposal from the forthcoming Hegotá upgrade, and has urged core developers to urgently prepare the network for quantum attacks by 2027.

On Wednesday, the group outlined “pqai27,” a proposed roadmap that aims to protect Ethereum against threats from quantum computing and artificial intelligence.

At Devcon, researcher Justin Drake said he hopes to complete the transition in 2028 while the published roadmap still targets December 2029.

Index provider MSCI has confirmed Bitcoin treasury company Strategy will be removed from its global equity indexes, following months of debate over whether crypto treasury firms qualify as operating businesses. Japan’s Metaplanet and crypto treasury company Upexi are also marked for deletion, while Ether treasury firm Sharplink is on a watchlist. The changes take effect after market close on Nov. 30.

“Index inclusion meant ordinary passive investors, like someone holding a global index fund in their pension, were getting leveraged Bitcoin exposure they never chose. MSCI just fixed that,” Ryan Kirkley, CEO of Global Settlement Network, told Cointelegraph. Strategy fell 6.49% on Thursday and are down by more than one quarter over the past month.

US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded $2.35 billion in net outflows over two consecutive weeks, as redemptions reached more than $1 billion each week.

According to Farside Investors data, spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $1.07 billion between from Monday to Friday, following $1.28 billion in outflows the previous week, the largest weekly redemptions since late June.

Friday marked the seventh consecutive trading session of net withdrawals, with about $1.71 billion redeemed since Nov. 5

At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 12.4% to trade at $65,116, Ethereum (ETH) is down 14.4% to trade at $1,822 and XRP (XRP) is down 13.3% to $0.96. The total market cap is at $2.2 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.

Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Kite (KITE) with a 35.5% gain, Pieverse (PIEVERSE) on 33.8%, and Midnight (CRV) on 28.7%.

The top three altcoin losers of the week are Zcash (ZEC) which was down 25.4%, Uniswap (UNI) down 23.2% and Aero (AERO) down 23.1%.

Bitcoin Opportunity Fund co-founder Mark Moss says that with banks and ETFs widening access to Bitcoin he expects a new record high in 2027. Wall Street’s embrace of Bitcoin has created the “best buying opportunity ever,” he said.

Microsoft managed to restore Microsoft 365 services after a massive global outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other applications for more than 24 hours, reiterating that the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack.

Microsoft said that the outage stemmed from a problem introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade that emerged after a recent network change. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents,” the company said.

MEGA, the organization behind Ethereum layer-2 network MegaETH, has reduced its workforce by 20% following months of restructuring as it expands into artificial intelligence products.

The layoffs come as MEGA shifts its focus toward developing products on the MegaETH network, including artificial intelligence services. The organization has committed $30 million to the initiative.

Metaplanet swung to a $170 million net loss in the first nine months of 2026, hit by a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings and a loss on the sale of 10,000 coins to demonstrate its ability to raise cash.

The Japanese company, the world’s second-largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, posted a net loss of 27.16 billion yen (about $170 million), compared with a profit of 13.53 billion yen ($84.6 million) in the same period last year. A 19.17 billion yen ($119.8 million) loss on the Bitcoin sale and an 8.04 billion yen ($50.3 million) loss from a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings outweighed gains in the operating business.

L1 blockchains Zilliqa, Gnosis and Ronin join the Ethereum ecosystem as the costs of going it alone grow, and the security and liquidity advantages become too hard to resist.

Ueno’s collapse exposed the fragility of digital banking in Paraguay, as customers scrambled for access to their money and stablecoins offered a lifeline.

Some Australian crypto investors are moving overseas to avoid the huge CGT increase from July 2027. But there are also less drastic ways you can pay less tax.

#4829. 6 Best Travel Dresses of 2026, Tested by a Style Writer and Travel Expert

Our top options are from Uniqlo and lululemon.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

The best travel dresses are the kind you can throw in a carry-on, forget about for hours, and still slip on looking put-together. As a style writer who’s constantly on the move (I checked off eight countries last year alone), I don’t say that lightly. I’ve learned the hard way which pieces wrinkle beyond the help of a hotel room iron, feel restrictive mid-transit, or just don’t pull their styling weight once I land. The ones worth packing work just as well with sneakers as they do with sandals, and make getting dressed in an unfamiliar place easy.

I tested 30-plus styles in real-life conditions, paying close attention to how they pack, wear, and hold up after long days of travel. The best ones strike the sweet spot between comfort and style with breathable fabrics, packable silhouettes, and just enough versatility to earn their spot in my very limited luggage space.

I’ve packed the below dresses for trips to Cancún, Paris, Marrakech, St. Lucia—and plenty of destinations in between—putting them through everything from long-haul flights to full-day itineraries. These are the ones I’ll reach for no matter where I’m headed next.

The Uniqlo Ultra Stretch AIRism Dress rings in at under $40, but the quality feels far more luxe. It’s smooth, polished, and super easy to style in a variety of ways for a single trip—meaning I can wear it multiple times without anyone clocking a repeat outfit.

The fabric is where this dress really shines, IMO. The signature AIRism material is made from 100 percent polyester, making it lightweight, breathable, and quick-drying with a soft, stretchy feel that moves with me. Whether I’m dealing with humid temps or long travel days, it keeps things cool and comfortable without clinging.

It also nails that easy, flattering fit-and-flare shape. It’s more fitted through the bust and subtly flares out toward the legs, creating a flowy drape that I especially love when walking—it just moves beautifully. The midi length hits at about mid-calf, striking that sweet spot between casual and pulled-together, so you can dress it up or down without overthinking it. I wore this dress to Barcelona during a warm September, and the breathable material and loose fit made it a major win.

And if you’re worried about packing a longer dress, don’t be. It packs down incredibly well, and any wrinkles from being in a backpack or suitcase shake out quickly before heading out the door. Plus, it has pockets! A huge win for travel days when you want to easily stash your phone, sunnies, or room key. The only downside: It’s unlined, so the white version is slightly sheer. But that also adds to its airy feel, and there are plenty of other color options if you want more coverage.

The updated lululemon Align Dress is a sporty option that can truly do it all. Designed with yoga in mind, it’s incredibly breathable, stretchy, and sweat-wicking—but doesn’t look overly athletic, thanks to its sleek, sporty-chic silhouette. It transitions seamlessly from a morning flow to a full day of sightseeing, making it one of those rare pieces I always throw into my suitcase.

The updated version improves on the original Align Dress with a nylon base and even more elastane, giving it more stretch and wrinkle resistance—yes, even after being packed down in compression cubes. Just like the brand’s famed Align leggings, this fabric feels ultra-smooth and lightweight.

Fit-wise, it features an A-line silhouette, meaning it's more fitted through the torso and gradually flares out toward the hem for a flattering drape. The mini length hits at about mid-thigh, keeping things cool and unfussy. Thoughtful built-ins like a shelf bra for light support and attached shorts with pockets make this dress perfectly practical and polished while on-the-go.

From a packing and styling perspective, it’s a no-brainer. The shorter length and featherlight fabric make it easy to toss into your suitcase and unpack with minimal wrinkles. I’ve styled it casually with a baseball cap and my fave travel shoe (shoutout to the Dr. Scholl’s Time Off Sneaker), but it also dresses up surprisingly well with a kitten heel and dainty jewelry. The only real downside is the price—it’s one of the most expensive picks on this list—but considering the quality, performance fabric, and versatility, it’s worth the investment (watch out, as it’s often on sale).

Stylish, short-sleeve dresses under $100 can be surprisingly hard to find. That’s why the Free People Blaine Midi Dress is one of my new faves. It offers just enough coverage (especially if your shoulders tend to burn in the sun like mine) while still keeping things breezy and cool. The overall vibe leans laid-back with that signature Free People look—think relaxed and boho but still put together.

Made from 100% cotton, the fabric is soft, breathable, and especially comfortable in heat and humidity. What I really love, though, is the subtly textured, crinkled finish paired with dramatic pleating, which keeps wrinkles at bay.

The fit is intentionally loose and billowy, giving it that airy, floaty shape the brand is known for. That said, its breezy fit means it runs large. My usual size worked, but I ended up using waist-cinching clips to create a bit more of a fitted shape, so I definitely recommend sizing down. It’s a midi-length dress that hits a few inches above the ankle, with thoughtful details like a stylish keyhole cutout at the back, and, yes, pockets.

This dress definitely leans casual, but in the best way. It’s great for daytime outings, exploring a new city, brunch, or even throwing over a swimsuit. I recently packed it for a trip to Mexico and it held up beautifully in the heat and humidity—easy, breezy, and styled perfectly with a simple sandal and a crochet bag.

This long-sleeve dress gives just the right amount of coverage on the arms but excels at breathability. That makes it perfect for everything from long-haul flights or bus rides to cooler evenings. It feels light and airy without sacrificing style, with an easy silhouette that still looks thoughtfully put together.

The fabric is a standout: a soft, gauzy 100% organic cotton that feels breathable and gentle against the skin. Like the Free People dress, it has a naturally textured, crinkled finish, so it doesn’t show wrinkles, even after being packed. Instead of pleating, it features a flouncy, tiered skirt with horizontal seaming, which adds movement and a bit of playful volume.

Fit-wise, it leans relaxed and slightly oversized, so sizing down is a smart move if you want a more tailored look. The mini length hits mid-thigh, creating a fun contrast with the long sleeves, while details like the subtle bell sleeves and button-down front upgrade the look. It’s one of those dresses that looks just as good styled casually as it does dressed up a bit.

It’s also incredibly versatile. The lightweight cotton makes it comfortable enough for daytime exploring while the longer sleeves give a little extra coverage when the temperature dips. It’s easy to throw on with sandals during the day or dress up with boots or jewelry at night—and just as easy to pack, thanks to that forgiving, wrinkle-resistant texture.

Meet the perfect mini dress. I own it in black, and it always looks incredibly chic—whether I’m dressing it up with heels for a city dinner or keeping it casual with sandals for daytime plans. It’s one of my favorite pieces because it feels polished no matter how you style it—coming in clutch for travel.

The fabric plays a big role in that versatility. It's made from a polyester crepe that has a subtle texture and is naturally wrinkle-resistant—ideal for tossing in a suitcase without a second thought. It holds its shape well and doesn't cling, giving it a clean, streamlined look straight out of your bag.

It has a classic, body-skimming silhouette that gently follows your shape without feeling tight or restrictive. The mini length hits at about mid-thigh, while the boat neckline adds a classy feel that instantly upgrades the overall look. It’s simple, but in that very polished, well-designed way.

It checks all the boxes for travel. The Bond Dress packs down easily, comes out looking polished, and can be styled in multiple ways depending on your itinerary. If there's a downside, it's that the streamlined fit doesn't leave much room for built-in functionality like shorts or roomy pockets, but the trade-off is a sleek, goes-with-anything mini you’ll reach for again and again.

The Dylan Mini Dress earns its spot as the most stylish pick thanks to its ultra-flattering shape and the prettiest range of colors and patterns. It has that slightly romantic feel that instantly dresses up your outfit, whether you’re heading to dinner or just wandering a new city. I always get compliments when I wear this dress (it was a major hit during my trip to Mallorca)—and it looks just as good in photos as it does in person.

The fit is where it really stands out. It has a flattering scoop neckline trimmed with delicate lace, plus a fitted bodice that dips slightly at the waist to help elongate your torso. From there, it flows into a long, airy skirt that moves beautifully as you walk. Adjustable straps let you customize the fit, and the built-in bra with removable pads adds support without the need for extra layers—always a win when packing light.

In terms of length, it hits a few inches above the ankles for that easy, breezy feel, and it comes in petite, regular, and tall options so you can find your ideal fit. The longer length gives it a slightly dressier edge, while still feeling relaxed enough for daytime wear. Despite the longer length, I don’t have any issues packing this dress in my suitcase when I pop it into a packing cube.

Style-wise, it leans pretty and girly in the best way. It’s perfect for summer travel or warm-weather destinations, but also transitions nicely into cooler conditions with a simple cardigan layered on top. The only con? Popular colors and patterns tend to sell out fast—so if you see a style available in your size, I recommend snagging it ASAP.

Since traveling involves lots of packing, travel expert Addie Bell says to look for wrinkle-resistant materials like spandex, nylon, or polyester. These fabrics are great for maintaining a polished look after being packed in a suitcase. Travel days often include a lot of walking, so you'll also want to make sure your dress's fabric is breathable—cotton and linen are great choices, but they are prone to wrinkling.

If you’re only traveling with a carry-on or trying to maximize storage, stick to neutral tones like black, navy, white, and beige, which are versatile and easy to mix and match with other wardrobe pieces. "Subtle patterns can also help hide wrinkles and stains, making the dress more travel-friendly," says Bell. But bright colors can add a fun, vibrant touch. "I always recommend sticking within a similar color palette to ensure they match other items you’re bringing.”

As a Women’s Health style writer, I travel during my PTO and I travel for work while scoping out destinations for WH’s Travel Awards. For the past few months, I’ve researched and tested the best travel dresses for jet-setting in style and comfort. In addition to testing dresses based on durability, material, style, and their ability to stand up to lots of movement and long hours, I also consulted travel expert Addie Bell, founder and CEO of Jetset and Travel, a travel consulting agency.

#4828. The 60 Best New Shows of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

We've got murder mysteries, stories of love and lust, and lots and lots of Yellowstone. And that's just the beginning.

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock)

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix)

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.
