#4700. Hydroxyapatite toothpaste promises to better protect your teeth. Here’s what the science says.

Published Nov 6, 2026 8:49 AM EST

There’s a new kid on the block in the toothpaste aisle. Next to the usual fluoride formulas, another option has been appearing: hydroxyapatite toothpaste.

Hydroxyapatite is the same mineral found in tooth enamel, and some claim using hydroxyapatite toothpaste can help plug tiny cracks in your teeth. Many brands are touting the new toothpaste as an effective alternative to fluoride. But does it actually protect your teeth, or is it just another trendy wellness product? After speaking with several experts, it seems like hydroxyapatite toothpaste might be worth trying.

Hydroxyapatite is a mineral made mostly of calcium and phosphorus that naturally occurs in human bones and teeth. It’s the main mineral in tooth enamel, the hard outer coating that helps protect your teeth from damage.

“Enamel is the hardest substance in the human body, but it’s not invulnerable,” says Dr. Joachim Enax, a chemist and senior scientist at Dr. Kurt Wolff GmbH & Co. KG, which makes hydroxyapatite toothpastes. Acids from foods and from bacteria in the mouth can gradually dissolve minerals from the tooth surface. Toothpastes that contain hydroxyapatite are designed to put some of that mineral back and help repair very early enamel damage, Enax explains.

If you’ve looked at these products, you may have seen labels mentioning “nano-hydroxyapatite” or “micro-hydroxyapatite.” That refers to the size of the mineral particles in the toothpaste. “Nano crystals are very fine and microscopic. Micro-hydroxyapatite crystals are larger,” says Dr. Hardy Limeback, a professor emeritus in the faculty of dentistry at the University of Toronto, who has been critical of fluoride use.

Both nano- and micro-hydroxyapatite occur naturally—for example, in breast milk—and because they are chemically the same as the mineral in tooth enamel, “they are added to toothpaste to plug up micro cracks or etches on the tooth surface,” he explains.

Hydroxyapatite toothpaste is not actually new. In the 1960s, research at NASA on growing crystals for electronics led to a patent for repairing teeth by growing hydroxyapatite crystals. A Japanese company later acquired the patent and introduced the first hydroxyapatite-based toothpastes in the 1980s.

Since hydroxyapatite was approved as an anti-cavity ingredient in Japan in 1993, similar toothpastes have become available in Europe (since 2006) and Canada (since 2015).

In the United States, you can buy hydroxyapatite toothpastes online and in some stores, but neither the Food and Drug Administration nor the American Dental Association has approved hydroxyapatite as an anti-cavity ingredient. To earn the ADA’s Seal of Acceptance—an official indication that a toothpaste helps prevent cavities—a product must contain fluoride.

Hydroxyapatite toothpaste can help remineralize enamel that has been weakened by acids from dental plaque or acidic foods, say Limeback and Enax. By promoting remineralization and forming a protective layer that helps shield enamel from acids, it may also protect teeth against cavities, says Dr. Elżbieta Paszyńska, a dental surgeon and head of the department of integrated dentistry and endodontics at Poznan University of Medical Sciences in Poland.

Fluoride prevents cavities in a similar way: Fluoride ions are incorporated into the enamel’s structure, helping repair very early decay and making the enamel more resistant to acid over time.

Paszyńska’s group ran two randomized clinical trials at two medical universities, with nearly 200 participants each: one in children aged three to seven, and one in adults with healthy teeth. For 12 to 18 months, participants used either a hydroxyapatite or a fluoride toothpaste. (Both studies were funded by Dr. Kurt Wolff GmbH & Co. KG.)

“At the end of both studies, children and adults using the hydroxyapatite toothpaste were no more likely to develop new carious lesions than those using fluoride toothpaste,” she says. “These findings demonstrated, in two independent clinical trials, that hydroxyapatite toothpaste can provide caries [cavity] protection comparable to fluoride toothpaste in daily oral care.”

Hydroxyapatite toothpastes may also help reduce tooth sensitivity by physically filling and sealing exposed dentinal tubules (the tiny channels leading to tooth nerves), Limeback and Enax note. In one study, people who used a nano-hydroxyapatite toothpaste for two to four weeks were less sensitive to cold air and touch than they had been at the start.

Early studies—most conducted in laboratory settings—suggest that regular use of hydroxyapatite toothpastes can also have a whitening effect. The mineral can form a thin, white layer on the tooth surface that helps mask the yellow tones of the underlying dentin and reduce the appearance of stains.

“This is different from bleaching; it is about restoring and maintaining the natural appearance of enamel,” Enax says. But more clinical trials are needed to confirm this effect in people.

Why our ancestors had straight teeth without braces

Is crossing your eyes really bad for you? We asked an optometrist.

In Europe, health officials have closely studied nano-hydroxyapatite in toothpastes and mouthwashes. In July 2025, the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety said this ingredient is safe in amounts up to about 30 percent in toothpaste and 10 percent in mouthwash. Most products on the market use 10 percent or less, which is well within that limit.

In the studies they reviewed, rod-shaped nano-hydroxyapatite did not damage DNA or harm cells, even when tested at high concentrations on mouth tissue samples in the lab. (The safety opinion does not apply to products that use needle-shaped particles.)

The committee concluded that any tiny amount of nano-hydroxyapatite particles that enter the cells lining the mouth is naturally removed from the body when those cells shed. If you swallow some toothpaste by accident, the particles are expected to break down quickly in stomach acid, causing no harmful effects.

Even with growing evidence in its favor, some U.S. dentists are cautious about swapping fluoride for hydroxyapatite.

“As far as telling someone, ‘Hey, stop using fluoride toothpaste and start using this,’ we don’t have enough evidence yet,” Dr. Hema Arany, a dentist and associate professor at the Medical University of South Carolina, said in a recent interview. “And so when it comes to standard of care, we are not recommending hydroxyapatite toothpaste.”

But some people avoid fluoride because they’re worried about possible links between fluoride and skin problems or neurodevelopmental issues in children, though these concerns remain debated and the data is still evolving. The World Health Organization and the American Dental Association maintain that fluoride toothpaste is safe and highly effective at preventing tooth decay when used as directed.

According to ethical guidance published in the Journal of the American Dental Association, for people who refuse to use fluoride, hydroxyapatite “is likely the second-best option.”

#4699. First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

#4698. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

#4696. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

#4695. Modernizing Nursery Rhymes for the 21st Century

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Back in the 1960s when I was growing up, nursery rhymes were an initial gateway to music for children. Their simple melodies, repeated lyrics, and predictable rhyming schemes gently introduced infants and toddlers to the fundamentals of music. What the words actually meant was of little, if any, concern to us young listeners. But times change and these traditional rhymes fell out of favor.

Revitalizing these classic verses—by preserving their developmental benefits while modernizing their themes—has become the life's passion of early childhood music educator Pam Gittleman. Raised in a musical family, Gittleman was a talented flutist through her college years. However, she did not plan on a career in music. After earning an MBA in marketing, she spent a decade in the corporate sector at a prominent advertising agency before leaving to raise her family.

Drawing on a desire to work with children, she leveraged her musical background to reinvent herself as a preschool music teacher. Over seven years at a summer day camp, she experimented with various teaching methods for children aged three to five, ultimately designing a curriculum centered on singing, movement, and call-and-response activities. As her own children grew up, she pivoted to teaching at nursery schools during the academic year.

Over the years, Gittleman noticed a striking trend: the young children in her classrooms were unfamiliar with the traditional nursery rhymes that prior generations knew by heart. Curious, she questioned parents and fellow educators and discovered that the internet had changed how families vetted content. Today’s parents were consulting childhood development experts and sharing their findings online. Many of them found traditional nursery rhymes to be outdated, dark, and inappropriate for young minds, so they avoided the genre entirely.

While recognizing the validity of these concerns, Gittleman’s professional training and instincts told her that the time-honored nursery rhymes still held value for teaching language skills as well as social and emotional intelligence. To bridge this gap, she began rewriting the lyrics.

Her venture received a major boost in 2020 when she enrolled in the year-long Advanced Leadership Initiative (ALI) at Harvard University. Despite pandemic-related disruptions, she had access to advanced graduate courses in education, thus establishing a firm theoretical foundation for how music and storytelling contribute to social and emotional learning (SEL) in early childhood.

Gittleman emphasizes that the linguistic structure of nursery rhymes is vital for early language acquisition. For instance, in the verses of “This old man, he played one, he played knick-knack on my thumb," children begin to learn the concept of rhyming. Educators can then challenge them to find other words that rhyme with "one," effectively expanding their vocabulary. Furthermore, because "one" and "thumb" don’t rhyme strictly speaking, children also learn that the concept of rhyming has flexibility.

Since many nursery rhymes are songs—set in a rhythmic structure and vocalized to musical notes—they stimulate important neurological pathways. Rhythm, for example, is processed simultaneously in the auditory and motor regions of the brain. Nursery rhymes capitalize on this connection, helping children regulate their motor functions through alternating periods of movement and rest. Gittleman notes that mastering this physical self-regulation translates to better behavioral and social functioning with others.1

Nursery rhymes can introduce basic math skills, too. Returning to the example of “This Old Man,” the song helps children learn to count, reaching ever higher numbers as they grow older. The rhymes are also repetitive—as children catch on to patterns, they learn to predict and reproduce them on their own. The excitement and anticipation of what comes next feeds the motivation and reward centers of the brain, allowing young children to experience joy while making music and learning language.

Yet another contribution of nursery rhymes is found in call-and-response verses. The call-and-response structure mirrors conversational patterns, teaching young children the social importance of taking turns.2

Equipped with decades of classroom experience along with academic knowledge obtained through her program at Harvard, Gittleman has systematically updated classic lyrics to be of service to social and emotional learning.3 Prioritizing kindness, empathy, and gratitude, she transformed "Three Blind Mice" to "Three Kind Mice" and, under her pen, the story of “Humpty Dumpty” has been reimagined so that when he falls off the wall his friends come to his aid, rather than leaving him in pieces on the ground.

Gittleman has since published several volumes of her work under the title Nursery Rhymes for Kinder Times®.4,5 These books feature engaging illustrations for young children and structured text to help growing children develop literacy skills. Pairing each rhyme with emojis and guiding questions, she provides adults with tools to enhance their children’s engagement with the stories while nurturing rich conversations that support emotional intelligence. When she introduced the curriculum to a local preschool, an informal survey of parents and teachers confirmed a positive impact on the children's social and emotional learning.6

Seeking to expand her reach, Gittleman utilized her advertising background to pitch her updated rhymes to the music industry. Her efforts won major support in 2022 when legendary children's performer Raffi—along with his protege, Lindsay Munroe—recorded 15 of her modernized rhymes. Since then, prominent children's recording artist Laurie Berkner has also recorded some of her material.

1 Williams, K.E. (2018). “Moving to the beat: Using music, rhythm and movement to enhance self-regulation in early childhood classrooms.” International Journal of Early Childhood, 50(1), 85-100. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13158-018-0215-y.

2 Wolf, D. (2017). “Why Making Music Matters,” research paper commissioned by Carnegie Hall. https://wolfbrown.com/wp-content/uploads/Why-Music-Matters.pdf.

3 Visit https://www.forkindertimes.com/ to learn more about Pam Gittleman’s work and products.

4 Gittleman, Pam (2023). Nursery Rhymes for Kinder Times, Volume 1. Herndon, VA: Mascot Books.

5 Gittleman, Pam (2025). Nursery Rhymes for Kinder Times, Volume 2. Herndon, VA: Mascot Books.

6 Gittleman adds that parents of bilingual learners found the rhymes particularly useful for enhancing their kids’ English skills.

#4694. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.
